analysis.one_liner: Bars members of Congress and their spouses from buying or selling individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee with zero cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit members of Congress and their spouses from buying or selling individual stocks while they hold office. Treasury bonds, index-style exchange-traded funds, mutual funds, and retirement-plan funds would still be allowed. Violators would face a fine of $25,000 per trade or the full value of the trade, whichever is higher, and the ethics office would publish compliance certificates online each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans gain a check on lawmakers trading on information learned in office. The public benefit is indirect but real: it reduces the chance that members are making decisions about industries they personally own stock in, and it addresses persistent public distrust over congressional stock trading.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from buying or selling covered securities, which include most publicly traded stocks [S2].

Allows continued investment in U.S. Treasury bills, notes, and bonds, exchange-traded funds, mutual funds, and retirement-plan investments, so members can still invest without picking individual companies [S2].

Imposes a fine equal to the higher of $25,000 per violation or the full value of the security traded, and requires an annual public posting of compliance certificates by the supervising ethics office [S2].
Extends the ban to spouses, closing the most commonly cited workaround in congressional stock trading [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest individual stock holdings and give up the ability to trade them while in office. There is no cost to taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The ban only covers individually picked securities; it leaves ETFs and mutual funds untouched, and those funds can still hold large positions in specific companies, so members could still hold indirect stakes in industries they regulate [S2].

A spouse who is employed can keep receiving securities as compensation from that employer after one year, creating an exemption that could shelter a working spouse's continued exposure to a single company [S2].

Enforcement runs through the supervising ethics office and a self-submitted pledge of compliance, with the fine set at $25,000 or the trade value; it does not add criminal penalties beyond existing law [S2].
The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, which an honest supporter would read as a signal that no cross-party coalition existed to move it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core policy is popular in principle and the fine is stiff, but the design is a blunt instrument: it bans picking stocks rather than requiring blind trusts or fuller divestment, and it leaves wide channels (funds, spouse compensation) through which members could keep market exposure. The larger obstacle was political, not technical: no other member of either party signed on, and the committee with jurisdiction never took it up.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 1, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which never scheduled it for consideration, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pat Fallon introduced the bill on November 1, 2023 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on House Administration, its only referral [S4].
The bill drew zero cosponsors in either party [S3].
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress keep the ability to buy and sell individual stocks, and their spouses keep theirs; the committee with jurisdiction avoided having to take a position on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who can still trade stocks

for.name: Rep. Pat Fallon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Insider Trading Prevention Act on November 1, 2023.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over member ethics rules
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup in the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House colleagues of both parties
against.role: All 434 other voting members of the House
against.what_they_did: No member cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the coalition needed to move it out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded vote, but the sponsor was a Republican and not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had no visible coalition on either side [S3].

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: The bill would force them to give up trading in individual stocks, a benefit of holding office that survives under current law. Their interest in keeping that ability runs against the transparency the bill would create.

industries.industry: Securities brokerages and retail trading platforms
industries.note: A ban covering 535 people would remove a small but well-resourced customer base from individual-stock trading. The effect is real but marginal for the industry overall.
